Family/split: Inform port and original TADS release share the same game/puzzles; keep them together. No existing Save Princeton entry found. Parent review required.

Use broker help for small excerpts only (at most the broker's 9 lines / 1000 characters); never read the complete guide into a worker prompt or replay it as a script. Save early at the first safe ordinary command prompt and at safe milestones, verify save success, and use checkpoints before risky probes. Answer active questions/keypauses first; for menus, Enter is an empty command string, not a literal space. On no_output_timeout use await_output only: do not send, retry, save, restore or restart while input is unresolved. Collect diverse explicitly labeled synthetic_probe cases with stated intent, including typos, wrong verbs, object naming and phrasing variations where meaningful, and verify actual intent-preserving repairs against observed output; no quota and no filler. Keep guided suggestions separate from observed evidence and preserve failed branches. Require actual author-intended finale with raw event IDs and quotes; death, quitting, chapter changes, partial scores and guide exhaustion never count. Private collection only; game and guide reuse permission unknown. No app changes, training, evaluation or publication. Parent must review provenance, final evidence and family/split concerns before export.

metadata.notes: Genuine author-intended winning ending, not death, quitting, or an intermediate score: the interpreter printed '*** You have won ***' with a perfect score of 200 out of a possible 200 and the rank 'Savior Of The University. Mazel tov!'. The narrative resolves the game's premise: the trumpet blast summons the student body, King Ash and his guard are bound and gagged, the office is restored, and President Shapiro congratulates the player. The two earlier deaths in this session (poisoned food e00122/e00606, unprotected headbutt e00294) were explicitly 'You have died' text undone via UNDO and are distinct from this conclusion. Full walkthrough completed (e00716, event index 716).
metadata.ending_quote:
You put the trumpet to your lips and blow it so hard that your earplugs pop out
. The noise that issues forth is thunderous, although it isn't enough to wake 
King Ash or his guard. It is enough, however, to summon most of the student 
body. Through the office window you see people pouring out of their dorms, 
giving fierce battle cries. Within moments, you hear a pounding on the outside 
of the office door. It shatters, and about fifty students flood into the room. 
While a few of them bind and gag King Ash and his guard, others dismantle the 
dais and scrape the crimson paint off the picture frames, restoring the office 
to its former layout.

Someone produces a case of champagne, and bottles begin popping. Professors, 
undergraduates, townspeople, and grad students all cluster around you, slapping 
your back and shaking your hand. Wandering among the crowd, you bump into such 
luminaries as George Schultz '43, Brooke Shields '87, and Jimmy Stewart '33. 
All of them want your autograph. You even receive a toast from F. Scott 
Fitzgerald '17, who has come back from the dead especially for this occasion.

Suddenly, the hubbub dies down, and you see President Shapiro gesturing for 
silence. He turns to you and puts a hand on your shoulder. "Superbly done," he 
says. "Now, please, I'll have to ask you all to leave. Before the invasion, I 
was filling out the university's tax records for fiscal 1991, and I simply 
can't wait to get back to them.


    *** You have won ***


In that game you scored 200 out of a possible 200, in 610 turns. This makes you 
Savior Of The University. Mazel tov!

# Save Princeton

Guide gives no release/serial and does not identify the Inform port; local story is R21/041125. Original TADS and Inform versions belong to the same family. Guide explicitly leaves small puzzles and guess-the-verb details unsolved.

Completion: Require the final office/King resolution with Hal and the trumpet and raw game output confirming Princeton is saved. Acquiring Hal, entering the office, solving a subpuzzle or guide prose alone is insufficient.

Family/split: Inform port and original TADS release share the same game/puzzles; keep them together. No existing Save Princeton entry found. Parent review required.

Use broker help for small excerpts only (at most the broker's 9 lines / 1000 characters); never read the complete guide into a worker prompt or replay it as a script. Save early at the first safe ordinary command prompt and at safe milestones, verify save success, and use checkpoints before risky probes. Answer active questions/keypauses first; for menus, Enter is an empty command string, not a literal space. On no_output_timeout use await_output only: do not send, retry, save, restore or restart while input is unresolved. Collect diverse explicitly labeled synthetic_probe cases with stated intent, including typos, wrong verbs, object naming and phrasing variations where meaningful, and verify actual intent-preserving repairs against observed output; no quota and no filler. Keep guided suggestions separate from observed evidence and preserve failed branches. Require actual author-intended finale with raw event IDs and quotes; death, quitting, chapter changes, partial scores and guide exhaustion never count. Private collection only; game and guide reuse permission unknown. No app changes, training, evaluation or publication. Parent must review provenance, final evidence and family/split concerns before export.

According to the brochure that the admissions department gave you, Princeton 
University is one of the last bastions of intellectual pursuit, where students 
can engage in the quest for learning unencumbered by worldly cares. As far as 
you can tell, though, the place looks like any one of a thousand clones of 
Cambridge University that clutter the American academic landscape. Still, you 
figure there must be something at least vaguely interesting about it, 
considering the reputation that the place has managed to accumulate over the 
past 250 or so years.

You decide, therefore, to take an Orange Key Tour. Minutes into it, though, you 
realize that you have no interest in being shown buildings with cannonball 
scars from the Revolutionary War. So, as the guide leads you through yet 
another archway, you break off from the group and wander through a nearby door. 
You find yourself in an entryway, standing in front of a door labeled with the 
number 21. When you turn the handle, the door swings open, and you enter, 
hoping no one will catch you being a voyeur.

As you poke around, the sound of gunfire coming from outside in the courtyard 
startles you. You dive for cover beneath a desk and remain there, shaking, 
until the tumult dies down. When you come out, you can sense a tension in the 
atmosphere. Clearly, something strange has happened.

events.response:
Special Commands

"Save Princeton" understands the following special commands:

"undo" may be used to take back your previous move.
"script" may be used to save a transcript of the game to a text file.
"unscript" turns scripting off.
"verbose" will cause the game to display the full description of every location 
that you enter, whether or not you have been there before.
"brief` will cause the game to only display the full description of a location 
if you have not seen it before. This is the default mode.
"oops" may be used to correct mistakes you have made in typing a command. For 
example:

> malk the cow
I DO NOT KNOW THE WORD "MALK"
> oops milk
BESSIE SIGHS CONTENDEDLY AS MILK SQUIRTS INTO THE BUCKET.

"Save Princeton" understands the following abbreviations:

"l" may be substituted for "look".
"x" may be substituted for "examine".
"g" may be substituted for "again".
"z" may be substituted for "wait".

events.intent: Read the basic instruction sheet for parser guidance
events.response:
WELCOME TO "Save Princeton"

"Save Princeton" is what is known as a "text adventure game." As you've already 
discovered if you've gotten far enough to read this message, the computer will 
describe for you various objects, locations, and characters. You can interact 
with them by typing in simple commands. For example, an exchange might go like 
this (with the computer's messages in all capitals, and your responses set off 
by ">"):
YOU ARE IN A WIDE FIELD. IN FRONT OF YOU IS AN ORNATELY CARVED BLACK STONE. 
PLUNGED INTO THE STONE IS A BEAUTIFUL SWORD.
> get sword
IT'S STUCK FIRMLY INTO THE STONE.
> examine sword
THE SWORD IS BEAUTIFULLY WROUGHT OUT OF GOLD AND SILVER, AND A PRECIOUS STONE 
IS SET IN ITS HILT.
> examine the stone
WHICH STONE DO YOU MEAN -- THE CARVED BLACK STONE OR THE PRECIOUS STONE?
> black
THERE SEEMS TO BE AN INSCRIPTION CARVED INTO IT IN GOTHIC LETTERING.
> read inscription
"WHOSOEVER REMOVES THE STONE FROM THIS SWORD IS RIGHTFUL KING OF BOISE."
> examine precious stone
IT'S SHAPED LIKE A POTATO.
> remove it from sword
THE PRECIOUS STONE POPS EASILY OUT OF THE SWORD. AS MAGICAL FIREWORKS BURST 
INTO THE SKY, A CHEERING THRONG OF FARMERS SURROUNDS YOU. A YOUNG FARMER -- 
BARELY MORE THAN A CHILD -- STEPS FORWARD AND PLACES A CROWN ON YOUR HEAD. 
"YOUR HIGHNESS," HE SAYS, "IT NOW FALLS UPON YOU TO DELIVER US FROM THE GREAT 
HAIRY MAN-MONSTER THAT HAS BEEN RAVAGING OUR FIELDS."

This dialogue illustrates a few basic points about how you communicate with 
"Save Princeton" or, for that matter, most other text adventure games. First, 
when you refer to an object, you don't need to be too detailed for the computer 
to figure out what you're talking about; notice how the player above only had 
to say "examine sword," not "examine the beautiful sword" -- although, as we'll 
see in a moment, either way would have worked equally well. However, when there 
are several possible objects that could fit your description, you'll need to 
give the computer enough information to know which one you're talking about. If 
you don't, the computer will ask for clarification, like it did when the player 
above referred to a stone but didn't specify which one.
Second, there can be several different ways to refer to the same object. When 
the player above told the computer to "get it," the computer remembered that 
the precious stone was the last object the player had mentioned.  Similarly, 
the following commands would all have one effect:
     > examine the young farmer
     > examine young farmer
     > examine child
     > examine the young child
Third, note that, in the sample dialogue, it was not immediately clear what to 
do with the sword. The player had to try a few different actions, and examine 
several items carefully, before it became obvious how to proceed. This will 
often be the case in any text adventure game you play. You will need to read 
anything readable, taste anything tastable, and smell anything smellable. 
Indeed, even if trying something crazy doesn't help you directly, it will often 
give you a clue on how to proceed. For example:

THERE IS GORILLA HERE, LOOKING OUT OF PLACE AMONGST THE BALES OF HAY.
> throw dictionary at gorilla
THE GORILLA GRABS THE BOOK IN MID AIR, LOOKS AT IT QUIZZICALLY, AND ATTEMPTS TO 
TAKE A BITE OUT OF IT. THEN, WITH A DISAPPOINTED ROAR, HE THROWS IT TO THE 
GROUND.

Aha! You've learned that the poor gorilla is hungry. And if you know that, 
earlier in the game, you saw a banana split back at the county fair, you could 
go back and get it. Of course, you might find that you'll have to find money to 
buy the dessert from Mrs. Jones. Sometimes, in a text adventure game, you'll 
need to solve one puzzle before you can solve another. At other times, puzzles 
will be independent of each other, and you'll be able to solve them in any 
order.
As you wander about, you will meet a number of characters. You can interact 
with them in a number of ways, but the most productive things to do with them 
will generally be to show them something, give them something, or ask them 
about something. For example:

FARMER BOB IS HERE, LEANING ON A PITCHFORK.
> ask bob about the pitchfork
FARMER BOB SIGHS AND SHAKES HIS HEAD. "OLD BESSIE'S BEEN FEELING MIGHTY USELESS 
LATELY, EVER SINCE THE CROP'S BEEN BRUNG IN."
> show the bale of hay to bob
FARMER BOB GRINS AND SAYS, "WHY, I'D PAY GOOD MONEY FER A FINE BALE OF HAY LIKE 
THAT."
> give hay to farmer
"THANK 'EE KINDLY," BOB SAYS, HAPPILY STICKING HIS PITCHFORK INTO THE BIG BALE 
OF HAY. HE TAKES A TEN DOLLAR BILL OF OF HIS OVERALLS AND HANDS IT TO YOU. 
"TAIN'T MUCH," HE SAYS APOLOGETICALLY, "BUT IT'S THE BEST I CAN DO."

Of course, you shouldn't limit yourself to just these three types of 
interaction. As always, trying something creative or even silly will often be 
useful, or at least entertaining:

"GET YOUR FRESH MEGA-BANANA SPLITS," MRS. JONES CALLS OUT. "JUST ELEVEN DOLLARS 
A SERVING!"
> give money to jones
"SORRY, DEARIE, YOU'RE A DOLLAR SHORT." MRS. JONES DECLINES YOUR MONEY.
> kiss jones
MRS. JONES GIGGLES AND TURNS BRIGHT RED. "WHY, BLESS YOUR HEART," SHE SAYS. 
"AND TO THINK I JUST PAID FIVE WHOLE DOLLARS FOR A KISS LIKE THAT AT THE 
KISSING BOOTH!"
> give money to jones
> MRS. JONES SIGHS. "AND TO THINK I THOUGHT YOU WERE BUSSING ME OUT OF THE 
GOODNESS OF YOUR HEART! WELL, I SAID IT WAS A FIVE DOLLAR KISS, AND I'LL STICK 
TO MY WORD. HERE YOU GO." SHE HANDS YOU A BANANA SPLIT AND FOUR DOLLARS CHANGE.

Sometimes, of course, situations will prove hazardous. The game will generally 
give you a warning -- or at least a hint -- before you do something deadly, 
unless you ought to know better on your own:

> examine the gorilla
THE GORILLA LOOKS ABSOLUTELY FEROCIOUS. I WOULDN'T GO NEAR IT, IF I WERE YOU.
> pat the gorilla
WELL, DON'T SAY I DIDN'T WARN YOU. AS YOU REACH OUT TO PAT THE CUTE, FURRY 
BEAST, IT REMOVES YOUR ARM WITH A SINGLE BITE. YOU PASS OUT FROM SHOCK. YOU DO 
NOT WAKE UP. YOU HAVE DIED.

If this little episode had come towards the very end of the game, you would 
probably be a bit frustrated at this point. In addition, sometimes you will 
destroy something that later turns out to be very important. There are two 
features to prevent you from having to start the game all over again just 
because you made one stupid mistake. First, there is an "undo" command that 
lets you take back your last move. You can undo up to one hundred of your most 
recent commands, but, if your mistake was made a number of moves ago, and you 
are only now discovering it, undo might not prove very useful. It is for this 
reason that "Save Princeton" has a "save" command. Typing "save" will cause the 
computer to take a snapshot of the game; the computer will remember every 
single move you've made up to the time that you save. If, at any later point, 
you wish to return the game to exactly the way it was at the time of the save, 
type "restore." You can save as many different snapshots of the game as you can 
fit on your disk.
Finally, a few details. You will notice a set of numbers on the top right hand 
side of the screen. This represents your score, and the number of moves you 
have made. For example, "20\234" would mean that you have a score of 20 points, 
and you have made 234 moves in the game so far. The move counter will go up 
just about any time you issue a command; the exceptions are when the computer 
won't execute a command (because, for example, you are trying to pick up an 
object that you already have) and when you command the game to do something 
outside of the story line, such as saving a game. The score counter will only 
go up when you have solved a puzzle, or made a significant step towards solving 
a puzzle.

Jacob sighs. "Eric told you to ask me that, didn't he?" he asks. "I know, I 
know, it's improbable that you should know the names of everything and 
everybody as soon as you see them. I considered having every character 
introduce him or herself when he or she first meets you, but I decided that 
that would be a pain to program, and a bore to play. So, just accept the fact 
that you have an invisible guide to campus, OK? It's just a game, anyway. It 
doesn't have to make complete sense."

all by ourselves."

As you enter, a bespectacled, middle-aged man looks up at you from the couch on 
which he sits. "Greetings," he says. "Am I correct in inferring that you have 
come as a veritable white knight to extricate me from the clutches of our 
mysterious invader? I should be honored to accompany you on your odyssey until 
such point as I may be restored to my proper position." You realize that this 
gratuitously polysyllabic man must be none other than Harold T. Shapiro, 
rightful president of Princeton University.

Lobby of Whig Hall
You are in a comfortable, if tastefully decorated, lobby. There is a bright 
yellow carpet, and a number of comfortable looking couches. I could describe it 
to you in greater detail, but neither of us wants that. After all, Whig is 
where the University's debate club is located, and who cares about a bunch of 
whiny pre-law types? Besides, it's getting close to the end of the game, and I 
assume you're as tired of detailed description as I am. And so, in place of the 
usual blather about the furniture here, I will simply remind you, speaking as a 
close friend concerned for the state of your conscience, that if you've gotten 
this far without sending the author a postcard, you ought to send one at once. 
Right now. Go ahead -- I'll wait for you.

Harold T. Shapiro is here, quietly cogitating.

"Mayhaps this would be an opportune moment to return to my office and oust the 
villains who seem to have taken over this bucolic campus," President Shapiro 
suggests.

events.response:
You put the trumpet to your lips and blow it so hard that your earplugs pop out
. The noise that issues forth is thunderous, although it isn't enough to wake 
King Ash or his guard. It is enough, however, to summon most of the student 
body. Through the office window you see people pouring out of their dorms, 
giving fierce battle cries. Within moments, you hear a pounding on the outside 
of the office door. It shatters, and about fifty students flood into the room. 
While a few of them bind and gag King Ash and his guard, others dismantle the 
dais and scrape the crimson paint off the picture frames, restoring the office 
to its former layout.

Someone produces a case of champagne, and bottles begin popping. Professors, 
undergraduates, townspeople, and grad students all cluster around you, slapping 
your back and shaking your hand. Wandering among the crowd, you bump into such 
luminaries as George Schultz '43, Brooke Shields '87, and Jimmy Stewart '33. 
All of them want your autograph. You even receive a toast from F. Scott 
Fitzgerald '17, who has come back from the dead especially for this occasion.

Suddenly, the hubbub dies down, and you see President Shapiro gesturing for 
silence. He turns to you and puts a hand on your shoulder. "Superbly done," he 
says. "Now, please, I'll have to ask you all to leave. Before the invasion, I 
was filling out the university's tax records for fiscal 1991, and I simply 
can't wait to get back to them.
